slides.title: Marketing creates value
slides.definition: Marketing is creating, communicating, delivering and exchanging offerings that have value for customers, partners and society (AMA).
bullets: Value comes from satisfying a need, not from the product itself
Maslow: customers prioritise lower needs before higher ones
Levitt: people buy a quarter-inch hole, not a drill
slides.example: Do we sell clothing, or a sense of belonging and self-esteem? Same product, different need served.
slides.trap: Thinking value is a product feature; value is the solved customer problem, which can sit at any Maslow level.
slides.memorise: Value = a need satisfied. Sell solutions, not products (Levitt's drill and hole).
slides.notes: Start with the AMA definition and notice the word 'value'. Value is not the thing you sell; it is the problem you solve for someone. Maslow's hierarchy gives you a map of the needs people are trying to satisfy, from safety to belonging to self-esteem. Levitt's line about the drill and the hole makes the same point: nobody wants the drill. This matters for the whole course because every AI tool we meet later, from synthetic research to personalised ads, is really a tool for finding and serving a need more precisely.

slides.title: Heterogeneity and STP
slides.definition: Customers differ in demographics, traits, experiences, purchase history and location, so we segment, target and position rather than treat everyone alike.
bullets: Segmentation: a small set of groups of similar customers
Targeting: pick segments by size, growth, alignment, competition – highest ROI
Positioning: how we want to be perceived versus competitors; identity is not image
slides.example: Nespresso group project: same machine sold to three segments with different Maslow needs and three different ads.
slides.trap: Confusing identity (what the brand says it is) with image (what customers actually perceive).
slides.memorise: STP sits between two extremes: treat all the same, or treat each differently.
slides.notes: Because customers are not the same, a firm faces two extremes: one message for everyone, or a different message for each person. Both are usually wrong or too costly, so marketers use STP. First find groups of similar customers. Then evaluate those groups on size, growth, fit with your strengths and competition, and target the ones with the best return. Finally position your brand against rivals in the customer's mind. Keep identity and image apart: identity is your intent, image is their perception. AI changes the cost of STP: synthetic research finds segments faster and dynamic creative lets you serve many more of them.

slides.title: The 4Ps and the funnel
slides.definition: The marketing mix is the tactical stage: Product, Price, Place and Promotion decisions that deliver the positioning.
bullets: Product: functionality, quality, packaging, brand, service
Price: list price, discounts, financing; Place: channels, logistics
Promotion: advertising, selling, PR – message, media, budget
slides.example: Course map: Promotion = S2–S5, Price = S6, Place/Service = S7. AIDA funnel (1898) and the customer journey describe the consumer side.
slides.trap: Mixing the marketing-mix 4Ps with Kopalle's dynamic-pricing 4Ps (People, Products, Periods, Places) in Session 6.
slides.memorise: 4Ps = Product, Price, Place, Promotion. AIDA = Attention, Interest, Desire, Action.
slides.notes: Once strategy is set, the 4Ps are the levers you pull. Product is what you offer, price is what you charge, place is how it reaches people, promotion is how you talk about it. The professor organises the course around these: promotion sessions first, then pricing, then customer service. On the consumer side, the purchase funnel, AIDA from 1898, and the modern customer journey with its physical and digital touchpoints describe how someone moves from unaware to buyer. Personas help you picture who is travelling that journey. Watch the trap: in Session 6 you meet a different set of 4Ps for pricing.

slides.title: Market research vs marketing analytics
slides.definition: Market research designs and collects data for a specific problem; marketing analytics constantly measures, monitors and analyses marketing performance.
bullets: Research: primary or secondary data, qualitative or quantitative
Analytics: dashboards, forecasting, optimisation, machine learning
Managers decide on experience, intuition and data – 'all others bring data'
slides.example: Session 2 (synthetic research) is market research; Session 8 (analytics, incrementality) is marketing analytics.
slides.trap: Treating them as the same function; research learns about the market, analytics monitors performance over time.
slides.memorise: Research = systematic study of a specific problem. Analytics = constant measuring and monitoring.
slides.notes: Firms learn about the market in two ways. Market research is a project: define a problem, design a study, collect and analyse data, report. It can use primary data you collect yourself or secondary data that exists already, and it can be qualitative, words and meanings, or quantitative, numbers. Marketing analytics is ongoing: dashboards, forecasts, optimisation and machine learning applied to the data the business generates every day. Both feed STP and the 4Ps. The course gives each its own session, so be ready for a question that asks you to tell them apart.

slides.title: AI: friend or foe?
slides.definition: AI creates clear opportunities for marketing but also threats; the professor wants a structured analysis, not a verdict.
bullets: Structure by marketing concept: strategy, marketing mix, research, analytics
Compare marketing with other functions; revenues with costs
Add the consumer side: behaviour and decision making
slides.example: Gartner: 65% of CMOs say AI will dramatically change their role within two years (reading).
slides.trap: Answering 'friend' or 'foe' with opinions only; marks come from structuring the impact across the course concepts.
slides.memorise: Structure the answer: strategy, 4Ps, research, analytics, consumer behaviour – opportunities and threats in each.
slides.notes: The opening question of the course is whether AI helps or harms marketing. The trick is not the answer but the structure. Walk through the concepts you have just learned: how AI changes strategy and STP, each of the 4Ps, market research and marketing analytics, and finally how consumers search, decide and buy. For each, list an opportunity and a threat. Compare marketing with other functions, and revenue effects with cost effects. The readings from BCG, Gartner and McKinsey give the numbers. This structure is the template for a big-picture exam question.

slides.title: The market research pipeline
slides.definition: Systematic design, collection and analysis of data for a specific marketing problem: define, design, collect, analyse, report.
bullets: Three research types: exploratory, descriptive, causal – rising certainty
Sampling: probability (random, stratified, cluster) vs non-probability (convenience, quota)
Costs come from participants, instrument design and analysis
slides.example: 'Is there a market for customised wine?' is exploratory; 'Do white labels raise sales?' is causal.
slides.trap: Descriptive research (who buys) is not the same as descriptive analytics in Session 8 (what happened).
slides.memorise: Exploratory → descriptive → causal as the problem gets clearer. Don't stop after analysis; recommend.
slides.notes: Market research is a project with five steps. You define the problem, design the study, collect data, process and analyse it, then report and turn it into actions. The type of research depends on how clear the problem is: exploratory when you only have a vague question, descriptive when you know the problem and want to describe who and what, causal when you can test whether a change causes an effect. Sampling matters because you study a subset and generalise to a population. Traditional research is expensive mostly because of participants, which is exactly the cost AI attacks.

slides.title: AI's four roles in research
slides.definition: AI can support existing methods, replace human data, fill gaps where humans are unavailable, or create research that never existed before.
bullets: Support: transcribe, code open-ends, draft surveys, summarise
Replace: synthetic participants instead of humans
Fill gaps and create new: niche segments, sensitive topics, digital twins
slides.example: Korst, Puntoni and Toubia (2025): the four-role framework on slide 21.
slides.trap: Digital twins belong to 'create new', not 'replace'; synthetic participants are the 'replace' role.
slides.memorise: Support · replace · fill gaps · create new (Korst, Puntoni & Toubia 2025).
slides.notes: Think of four levels of ambition. At the lowest, AI speeds up what researchers already do: transcribing interviews, coding open answers, drafting questions. Next, AI replaces the human respondent with a synthetic one. Third, AI fills gaps where human data is hard to get: tiny segments, stigmatised topics, rapid concept screens. Fourth, AI creates new research types, especially digital twins that let you test strategies on a virtual replica of a real customer. The exam loves the mapping: synthetic participants are 'replace', digital twins are 'create new'.

slides.title: Participants vs digital twins
slides.definition: A synthetic participant is an LLM answering as a prompted persona; a digital twin is calibrated on one real person's actual prior answers.
bullets: Participant: persona by age, gender, income, attitudes; scales to thousands instantly
Twin: predicts how that same person responds to new stimuli
Twin uses: 'first impression twice', fixed-panel tracking, what-if simulation
slides.example: Slide 36 prompt: 'You are a consumer aged 40–50, female, Singapore… repeat 100 times as a new consumer.'
slides.trap: Calling a richly described persona a digital twin; a twin needs real human data from that specific person.
slides.memorise: Twin accuracy depends entirely on the richness and recency of the human data it was calibrated on.
slides.notes: Both are LLM-based, but the source of truth differs. A synthetic participant starts from a description: tell the model who to be and it answers in character, and you can repeat that a thousand times. A digital twin starts from a real person: you feed the model that person's past survey or interview answers so it can predict how they would react to something new. That gives you a longitudinal panel with zero attrition and fast what-if testing. The catch is that a twin is only as good as the human data behind it, and people change.

slides.title: The four cons
slides.definition: Synthetic answers suffer hallucination, bias amplification, regression to the mean and trained behaviour, so validity is the central worry.
bullets: Hallucination includes misreading the prompt: 'more expensive = higher quality?'
Bias amplification exaggerates stereotypes; regression flattens to average internet opinion
Trained behaviour: harmlessness and fairness tuning makes answers polite
slides.example: PNAS 11–20 game: LLMs reasoned less deeply than humans and their answer distribution did not match.
slides.trap: Swapping bias amplification (exaggerates differences) with regression to the mean (erases differences).
slides.memorise: Hallucination · bias amplification · regression to the mean · trained behaviour.
slides.notes: Four things go wrong. First, the model invents facts and can even misinterpret your prompt. Second, it leans on stereotypes in its training data and makes them stronger. Third, it reports the average opinion of the internet, so real variety between people disappears. Fourth, it has been trained to be harmless and fair, so it is politer and more agreeable than real respondents. The PNAS paper tested this with the 11–20 money game and found LLMs less human-like, with unstable results across models and task wording. The professor's conclusion: apply but remain cautious.

slides.title: Prompting techniques and their limits
slides.definition: Zero-shot tricks, few-shot examples, RAG and fine-tuning were tested as ways to make LLM answers more human-like.
bullets: Zero-shot (chain-of-thought, roles, demographics): not more human-like, unstable
Few-shot: answers driven by the samples given; parameters unchanged
RAG: closer but still different; fine-tuning: human-like, not significantly different
slides.example: Slide 37 steering instructions: 'treat each consumer as independent… allow some to reject EVs' – or does that steer too much?
slides.trap: Thinking RAG updates the model; only fine-tuning changes parameters. And if you fine-tune on human data, why simulate it?
slides.memorise: Fine-tuning made LLMs human-like; RAG helped; zero-shot and few-shot did not.
slides.notes: Researchers tried to close the gap between LLM and human answers. Prompt tricks like chain-of-thought, assigning a role or adding demographics did not help and gave unstable results. Giving sample answers, few-shot, just made the model copy the samples. Giving it the original paper through retrieval made answers more human-like but still different. Only fine-tuning, updating the model on many human answers, removed the significant difference. That raises the professor's awkward question: if you already have the human data to fine-tune, why would you need synthetic participants? Also note the steering dilemma: instructions to vary respondents reduce bias but may steer too much.

slides.title: How search engines rank
slides.definition: Engines crawl and index the web, then rank indexed pages on two pillars: relevance to the query and importance from inbound links.
bullets: Relevance: overlap between query and page text, weighted, length-controlled
Importance: number and quality of incoming links (a Forbes link helps)
Other signals: click-through (+), suspicious link jumps (−), malware, slow load (−)
slides.example: Same content on the World Bank site and 'Jason's blog': the engine prefers the World Bank's higher importance.
slides.trap: Importance is not keyword count; it is link authority. Relevance is the text match.
slides.memorise: Two pillars: relevance (text match) and importance (inbound links and their quality).
slides.notes: A search engine does not search the live web. It crawls from trusted seed sites, follows links, stores and indexes content, then answers queries from that index. To decide what to show it uses two pillars. Relevance asks how well the page text matches the query, weighting some words more and controlling for page length. Importance asks how many sites link to the page and how important those sites are. Other factors nudge rank: click-through helps, suspicious link spikes, malware and slow loading hurt. SEO is the craft of improving both pillars without paying the engine.

slides.title: Query types and SEO basics
slides.definition: Searches are informational, transactional or navigational, roughly matching journey stage; SEO builds relevance on-page and importance off-page.
bullets: Informational: 'best baby stroller'; transactional: 'buy coffee machine online'; navigational: 'dbs contact number'
On-page SEO: keyword research, helpful content around those keywords
Off-page SEO: promote content to earn links from other sites
slides.example: Google Trends for keyword research; 'anniversary gift ideas' as a non-obvious keyword.
slides.trap: Labelling a brand-plus-manual query as informational; a specific site or document is navigational.
slides.memorise: Informational → transactional → navigational. On-page = relevance; off-page = importance.
slides.notes: People rarely type a website address; they use search. Their queries fall into three types that line up with the customer journey: informational early on, transactional when ready to buy, navigational when they already know where to go. SEO works both pillars. On-page, you research the keywords people use and write genuinely useful content around them, ideally different from competitors. Off-page, you promote that content so other sites link to it, which raises importance. Paid search buys a position instead; SEO earns it.

slides.title: What GEO optimises
slides.definition: GEO improves visibility inside LLM answers: being included, share of words, position-adjusted word count, impression and being recommended.
bullets: Two developments: learning without visiting websites; bots as customers
LLMs are used for early information search; engines for targeted transactional search
Two challenges: be retrievable (technical) and be included (content)
slides.example: Puntoni (2026): customers ask the LLM and never visit the site the answer relied on.
slides.trap: Saying GEO optimises rank; rank is SEO. GEO's metrics are inclusion and share of the answer.
slides.memorise: GEO optimises inclusion, word share, position-adjusted word count, impression, recommendation.
slides.notes: Two things changed. First, people learn from the LLM's answer and often never click through, so your website may never be seen. Second, bots increasingly make the decision for the customer. That means the goal shifts from ranking on a results page to being inside the answer. Aggarwal and colleagues measure this as whether you are included, how many words you get, how early you appear, and the subjective impression of relevance and uniqueness, plus whether the LLM recommends you. Technically you must be crawlable; content-wise you must be worth quoting.

slides.title: Does SEO still work? What does?
slides.definition: On-page relevance still matters but keyword stuffing hurts; backlinks have a weak direct effect; being discussed beats being linked.
bullets: Top techniques: add quotations, add statistics, cite sources
Good techniques: fluency, technical terms, authoritative, easy to understand
Technical: crawlable, don't block good AI crawlers, semantic HTML, low latency
slides.example: Aggarwal et al. (2024): best technique gives 41% improvement in position-adjusted word count, more for lower-ranked sites.
slides.trap: Listing keyword stuffing or buying backlinks as GEO tactics; both are ineffective or harmful.
slides.memorise: Quotes, statistics, citations work; 41% lift; keyword stuffing hurts; discussed beats linked.
slides.notes: The professor's answer is yes and no. Relevance still matters, so useful on-page content helps, but stuffing keywords produces low-quality writing that LLMs do not quote. Links have only a weak direct effect; what matters is being discussed across the web, so the model has passages about you to retrieve. The KDD paper tested techniques and found three winners: adding quotations, adding statistics and citing sources, with fluency and authority as good supporting moves. The best technique lifted position-adjusted word count by 41 percent, with bigger gains for sites that ranked lower. Technically, keep the site crawlable and fast; special AI files are not needed.

slides.title: Iterative method and beyond GEO
slides.definition: Use the LLM as a simulated customer: feed your and competitors' content, ask for a recommendation, revise, repeat; then think about agents.
bullets: No waiting for market response, unlike SEO; add guardrails against false claims
Beyond GEO: brand-owned agents vs third-party agents choosing for consumers
Agent-to-agent interaction, a dual internet, maybe paid LLM recommendations
slides.example: State Property went from last to first in one revision by adding a founder quote, a market statistic and cited sources.
slides.trap: Fixing a real product gap with copy; the exercise showed speed was a product problem, not a writing problem.
slides.memorise: Iterate with the LLM as judge; keep claims true. Acar & Schweidel: prepare the brand for agentic AI.
slides.notes: Inspired by Hosanagar, the iterative method turns the LLM into a test customer. Give it your write-up and your rivals', restrict it to that content, pose a customer scenario and ask it to recommend one. Read why you lost, revise, and ask again. In class, State Property moved from unrecommended to first choice in one round, but a stress test with a ten-week deadline exposed a genuine speed gap that honest copy could not fix. Looking ahead, brands may offer their own agents, or compete inside third-party agents, raising questions about branding, price and whether humans still need a website.

slides.title: Old workflow: strengths and weaknesses
slides.definition: Brief, strategy and concept, production, media planning and buying, measurement: five steps run by an agency over weeks or months.
bullets: Strength: human nuance, culture, humour, big-idea campaigns
Weakness: each cycle takes weeks; assets are expensive
Weakness: testing is costly, so little experimentation
slides.example: Advertising is the push side of Promotion; SEO/GEO (S3) is pull. You still advertise to create demand that GEO later captures.
slides.trap: Advertising and SEO/GEO are not substitutes: one creates demand, the other captures it.
slides.memorise: Five steps: Brief → Strategy & Concept → Production → Media Buying → Measurement.
slides.notes: Think of the old agency model as a slow, expensive factory. A client writes a brief, planners find a big idea, a crew produces one polished asset, the agency buys media, then a report arrives weeks later. Its strength is human craft and cultural feel. Its weakness is speed and cost: you cannot make many versions or test much. Keep in mind the push versus pull distinction with Session 3. Ads push a message to people not yet looking; SEO and GEO pull in people already searching. Cutting ads slowly drains the pool that search later fishes from.

slides.title: Replacement vs new opportunities
slides.definition: Gen-AI does two things: it replaces parts of the existing workflow, and it creates options that did not exist before.
bullets: Replace: copy variants, image/video assets, bid optimisation, live measurement
Create: co-creation, mass customisation, hyperpersonalisation
In-house teams rose from 42% (2008) to 82% (2023)
slides.example: Coca-Cola Create Real Magic (co-creation); Nutella Unica, 7 million unique jar labels (mass customisation).
slides.trap: Nutella Unica is mass customisation, not hyperpersonalisation: the label is unique but not tied to a known person.
slides.memorise: Hyperpersonalisation = the specific variant is tied to an identifiable person or micro-segment.
slides.notes: Kim calls this a paradigmatic evolution, not just new tools. On the replacement side, LLMs write dozens of headlines, image tools make cheap assets, and platforms optimise bids and measure continuously. On the creation side, three new things appear. Co-creation invites consumers into the story, like Coca-Cola's art contest. Mass customisation produces huge numbers of unique variants, like Nutella's seven million labels. Hyperpersonalisation goes one step further: a specific variant for a specific identifiable person. The risk of all this cheap output is drift toward generic, average language and loss of brand consistency, which is why prompting becomes a strategic skill.

slides.title: Static personalisation vs DCO
slides.definition: Static: variants or swap rules are fixed before serving. DCO: modules are assembled per impression in real time, with brand elements locked.
bullets: Lock logo, colours, fonts; vary image, headline, offer, CTA
Static rules are set in advance (show last-viewed product)
DCO learns which combination works as ads keep serving
slides.example: Meta Advantage+ (2022) automates targeting, placements and creative versions; Meta claims about 22% higher return on ad spend.
slides.trap: Many pre-made variants are still static. DCO means the platform assembles the ad per impression.
slides.memorise: Static = rules before serving; DCO = assembled per impression, brand locked, learned over time.
slides.notes: Almost every module of an ad can change: headline, copy, hero image, product, offer, tone, format, even the landing page. What you never change are the core brand elements. In the static approach you decide the swaps in advance, either by producing many versions or by a fixed rule like showing the last product viewed. Dynamic creative optimisation breaks the ad into slots, fills each from an approved pool, and lets the platform assemble the best combination for each person in real time, learning from results. Gen-AI's job is to fill that pool cheaply; the human job is to set the objective and lock the brand.

slides.title: The AI ad perception gap
slides.definition: Advertisers believe young consumers like AI ads far more than they do; disclosure is where both sides agree.
bullets: 82% of executives think consumers are positive; only 45% are
Gen Z 39% negative vs Millennials 20%
73% say disclosure would raise or not change purchase likelihood
slides.example: IAB 2026: Gen Z call AI-using brands inauthentic (30%), disconnected (26%), unethical (24%). Top advertiser benefit shifted to cost efficiency (64%).
slides.trap: The gap widened because advertisers' concerns turned inward (cost, creativity), not because consumers warmed up.
slides.memorise: 82% vs 45%; Gen Z 39% negative; disclosure is the bridge (73%).
slides.notes: Advertisers judge AI by internal benefits like cost and speed. Consumers judge by how an ad feels. That is why the gap is 37 points and widening. Gen Z is the most sceptical group and uses words like inauthentic and unethical. The IAB warns that chasing cheaper rather than better content risks AI slop. The one point of agreement is disclosure: most young consumers want it, most executives support it, and nearly three quarters say knowing an ad was AI-made would not reduce their purchase likelihood. Disclosure matters most for video, images, and for pharma, political and financial ads.

slides.title: Agency vs in-house with AI
slides.definition: ChatGPT lifts the floor, not the ceiling. The agency model must shift from making ads to designing the system that makes ads.
bullets: In-house pros: speed, low cost, freedom to experiment
Cons: weaker storytelling, consistency, IP and legal risk
70% of marketers have had at least one AI incident (IAB 2025)
slides.example: Timperio: AI-only was cheapest per interaction ($0.0046) and earned most likes; agency about 3.6x cost once its 350 euro fee is counted.
slides.trap: AI-only did not win everything: the agency clearly won informative images; format (reels) mattered more than who made the ad.
slides.memorise: Hybrid: AI in-house for volume, humans for flagship work, human review before publishing, disclose.
slides.notes: The provocative question is why hire an agency when ChatGPT can do the job. The answer is that AI makes competent output available to everyone, but agencies still add the big idea, brand consistency over years, cultural taste, media negotiation and accountability when things go wrong. Timperio's experiment supports a hybrid: AI handles everyday reels and seasonal content cheaply, humans handle product-accurate and flagship pieces. Given that seventy percent of marketers have already had an AI incident, keep human review, brand checklists and documented prompts. Agencies will move to selling strategy, AI orchestration, governance and measurement rather than hours.

slides.definition: An influencer has a large, engaged following you would not know unless you followed them (Haenlein et al., 2020). Brands borrow their trust.

slides.notes: Attention is scarce. People spend more time on social media and brands compete with friends, creators and entertainment, not just other brands. A virtual influencer is a computer-generated character with a personality, backstory and social accounts, realistic or cartoon-like. It says only what it is told, looks the same every time, and can appear in five places at once in any language. Two ownership models matter for the exam: independent characters like Miquela, run by a studio, and brand-owned characters like Lu, where the retailer keeps all the equity and even uses her for customer service. Success is not the image; it is the team, the story and continuous investment.

slides.title: Paid vs organic engagement
slides.definition: Virtual influencers' paid posts earn more engagement than their organic posts (+13.3%); human influencers' paid posts earn less (-2.1%).
bullets: Humans lose authenticity when paid; virtuals have none to lose
Brand deals add novelty and production polish
Fashion and beauty strongest: +16.3% vs -2.3%
slides.example: HBR (Hwang et al., 2024): 551 human and 13 virtual influencers, 112 brands, over 1M posts, 2014 to 2020.
slides.trap: Do not flip the signs: virtual up, human down. It is engagement, not reach; humans still have 2.8M vs 1.1M followers.
slides.memorise: +13.3% virtual vs -2.1% human on paid posts; no authenticity to betray.
slides.notes: This is the counter-intuitive finding the professor is most likely to test. Followers expect a human to be real, so a sponsored post feels like selling out. A virtual influencer is already understood as a brand creation, so an ad is no betrayal. Paid collaborations also give the character new, surprising content, like Miquela with BMW, and bigger production budgets. Fashion and beauty are image-led, which CGI does well. The implication is that disclosure does not kill performance for virtual influencers, and that brands should run a portfolio: humans where lived experience matters, virtuals for high-concept or risk-sensitive campaigns.

slides.title: Authenticity: the CMR triad
slides.definition: Authenticity is judged from a set of signals: information credibility, disclosure transparency and reputation trust, working together.
bullets: Effect is multiplicative: one or two signals feel hollow
All three present under 9% of the time, then 82% success
Labels must be understandable: Meta moved to clickable AI Info
slides.example: Vodafone Germany's AI presenter was spotted by a moving mole; admitting the experiment turned a crisis into a conversation.
slides.trap: Any one signal is not enough; the triad multiplies. A blunt label (Made with AI) backfired.
slides.memorise: Credibility x transparency x reputation; disclose clearly; only 15% highly trust AI influencers.
slides.notes: Saxena calls today the Perceived Era: when AI can fake anything, people judge what is real from several cues at once, about four on average. Three matter most. Can I check your facts? Are you clear about AI use, in plain words? Do you have a good track record? The effect multiplies, so a brand with credible facts but hidden AI use still feels suspicious. The uncanny valley adds a design rule: go clearly stylised or fully polished, because almost-human with glitches is the danger zone. Disclosure is becoming law under the EU AI Act and platform policy, and getting found out costs more than disclosing.

slides.title: Ethics and the build pipeline
slides.definition: Virtual influencers raise representation and deception concerns, and building one is quick; making it trustworthy is the real work.
bullets: Risk: renting diversity (Shudu), unrealistic bodies, undisclosed fakes
Mitigate: involve real creators, disclose, avoid impossible ideals
Pipeline: image (save the seed) > script > voice > animate > edit
slides.example: Nars dropped a human influencer after drama and launched three virtual ones; Ralph & Russo's Hauli earned 19.4M views.
slides.trap: Virtual influencers can widen representation (human pool 68% white); the issue is who controls and profits.
slides.memorise: Coexistence, not replacement: portfolio of humans and virtuals; save prompt, settings and seed.
slides.notes: Two ethical worries recur. First, a brand can rent diversity without paying real people from that group; Shudu was created by a white male photographer. Second, young followers may not realise the character is fake, and most virtuals are young, thin and female. The balanced answer is that the character itself is not the problem; control, credit and disclosure are. On the build side, the class pipeline was Leonardo for the face, a short script, ElevenLabs for voice, Vidnoz or HeyGen to animate, CapCut to crop and caption. Save the seed so the face stays consistent. The conclusion from every reading is coexistence: humans and virtuals in a portfolio.

slides.notes: Read the ladder left to right. Rules are blind. ML predicts but each prediction stands alone. RL acts, gets a reward and plans for the week. The last box is the management layer: price floors and caps, banned data types, crisis switches and disclosure. The algorithm learns what works; people decide what is fair.

slides.title: Kopalle's four Ps of dynamic pricing
slides.definition: Dynamic pricing means prices change with four demand drivers: People, Products, Periods, Places. Static pricing is the case where none vary.
bullets: People: who has higher willingness to pay
Products: configuration (first class, bundles); Periods: surge, markdowns
Places: outlets, regional prices; the law of one price fails
slides.example: Hyderabad vegetable seller: rich areas first, poorer areas cheaper later, wilting stock near cost; one cart, all four Ps.
slides.trap: Not the marketing-mix 4Ps (Product, Price, Place, Promotion). Kopalle: People, Products, Periods, Places.
slides.memorise: People, Products, Periods, Places; surveillance pricing = people-based pricing on personal data.
slides.notes: Price is the only P that earns money directly. History circles from haggling to one public price, John Wanamaker's price tags in 1876, and back to individual prices powered by data. Kopalle's paper defines dynamic pricing by four demand drivers that all begin with P: who is buying, what configuration, when, and where. Surge pricing, markdowns, outlet stores and personalised offers are all cases of it. The critical name for people-based pricing on tracked personal data is surveillance pricing. Firms do it to capture willingness to pay, allocate scarce stock, personalise, and keep up with rivals.

slides.title: Data, ML and reinforcement learning
slides.definition: Rules are blind; ML predicts one-off outcomes from history; RL learns a policy by acting, getting rewards and planning for the long run.
bullets: Data: own, partner, broker; non-personal (rivals, weather) vs personal (browsing, loyalty)
RL loop: state > action > reward > improve the policy
Explore (try prices) vs exploit (use the best known); bandits, A/B tests
slides.example: Roast & Reward: 5,000 cups a week, $1 cost, $1.50 Sunday waste penalty; the ML adviser ignores stock pacing.
slides.trap: RL is not ML with more data: RL decisions are sequential, today's price changes tomorrow's stock.
slides.memorise: ML = independent predictions; RL = agent, environment, state, action, reward, policy, long-run cumulative reward.
slides.notes: Firms climb a ladder. Heuristics are simple if-then rules. Machine learning learns patterns from past data and predicts demand or willingness to pay, one prediction at a time. Reinforcement learning is different: an agent sets a price, observes the profit, and updates its policy to maximise total reward over time, because selling cheap on Monday empties the stock you need on Saturday. The core trade-off is explore versus exploit: explore more early, exploit later, keep a small share exploring because markets change. Firms use A/B tests and multi-armed bandits. Kopalle notes most firms still have humans approve suggestions.

slides.title: Legal and ethical limits
slides.definition: Market-data pricing (periods, places, products) is accepted; people-based pricing on personal data breaks trust and is now regulated.
bullets: Delta 2025: announced AI fares, backlash, promised no personalised fares
Uber Sydney siege: 4x surge in a crisis, 'the wrong decision'
RealPage: shared algorithm with private data looked like price-fixing
slides.example: New York: 'THIS PRICE WAS SET BY AN ALGORITHM USING YOUR PERSONAL DATA'; Connecticut: visible notice when data raises a price.
slides.trap: Perception alone can hurt: Delta never implemented personal fares yet still had to back down.
slides.memorise: Delta = perception; Uber = crisis circuit breakers; RealPage = algorithmic collusion; firms stay responsible.
slides.notes: Three warning cases carry the lesson. Delta only said it would use AI revenue management and the public assumed personal fares, so it had to promise Congress it would not. Uber's surge during a hostage crisis was economically logical and morally tone-deaf, so firms need caps that switch off in emergencies. RealPage shows that rivals feeding private data into one tool can collude without talking, and the firms, not the vendor, are responsible. Regulators are moving, led by US states with disclosure laws, and the EU already requires telling people when a price is personalised. The FPF guide gives a seven-step playbook: map data, test bias, allowed and never-allowed data, disclose, real baselines, protect essentials, align vendors.

slides.title: Framing: discount vs surcharge
slides.definition: The same money outcome feels fair as a discount and unfair as a higher personal price, because people believe a fair reference price exists.
bullets: '$20 off' keeps the $140 reference; a gain
'Your price $120, theirs $100' breaks it; feels like discrimination
Baseline must be real: fake 'was' prices are deceptive
slides.example: Kopalle: shelf price $2,000 plus a $400 coupon to the price-sensitive group equals the optimal two prices.
slides.trap: Framing does not make it a different price; it changes the feeling. Inflated list prices are illegal deception.
slides.memorise: Personalise discounts, not prices, from a bona fide baseline; laws target price increases.
slides.notes: Prospect theory says losses hurt more than gains. If I learn my price is twenty dollars higher than yours, I feel a loss against a fair reference. If we both see the same list price and I get a smaller coupon, I still feel I gained. That is why disclosure laws target increases and why firms will move to discount framing. The practical rule is to set a real list price and personalise the discounts. The warning is that some sellers inflate the list price to make discounts look bigger; that is deceptive and consumers react badly when they find out. Dubé himself gives the same example with two prices for the same six-pack.

slides.title: Who wins, who loses: ZipRecruiter
slides.definition: Dubé and Misra's field experiment: the firm gains a lot, consumers as a group lose a little, but most individual customers are better off.
bullets: Best uniform price $99 to $327: profit +55%
Personalised prices: +19% more; total consumer surplus falls
Over 60% of individuals better off, mostly smaller firms
slides.example: 7,867 new customers, ten random prices from $99 to $399, then an out-of-sample test on new customers.
slides.trap: The +55% came from fixing the single price, not from personalisation; personalisation added only +19%.
slides.memorise: +55% uniform, +19% personalised, >60% better off; backlash and ability-to-pay are not in the model.
slides.notes: The biggest win was boring: ZipRecruiter was simply underpriced, and raising one price for everyone lifted profit by more than half. Personalisation added a smaller gain on top. Total consumer surplus fell, yet more than sixty percent of customers paid less than the uniform price, mostly smaller and less advantaged firms, so fairness-weighted welfare can even rise. The critics in the American Prospect reply that this prices on willingness, not ability, to pay and historically hits the poor, as with Staples and broadband. The authors admit one B2B monopoly case and no long-term backlash. Also, consumer surplus is non-monotonic in data, so removing data can hurt consumers.

slides.title: Rule-based vs AI chatbots
slides.definition: Rule-based bots follow decision trees with pre-written answers. AI chatbots use generative models, understand open input and keep context.
bullets: Rule-based: deterministic, same input gives same output
No match means 'Sorry, I didn't understand that'

slides.example: IVR phone trees ('press 1 for...') mocked since 1993; ELIZA in the 1960s; generative AI and voice agents from 2022.
slides.trap: Thinking Gen-AI solved everything. 77% are still frustrated and 88% prefer a human (HBR).
slides.memorise: Rule-based = decision tree, predictable, breaks on phrasing. AI = generative, probabilistic, keeps context.
slides.notes: Picture an old phone menu: press 1, press 2. That is a rule-based bot. It is easy to audit and totally predictable, but it breaks the moment you say something it did not expect, so you get the dreaded 'please rephrase' loop. An AI chatbot is built on a generative model. It copes with typos and slang, handles two requests in one sentence, remembers what you said three turns ago, and can summarise the chat for a human agent. Adoption jumped from about 5% of service teams in 2020 to over 80% in 2025. Yet customers are still frustrated, which tells you the remaining problems are not technical.

slides.title: Two problem groups
slides.definition: Chatbot problems split into understanding and complexity, and handover, humanisation and personalisation. AI fixed the first group more than the second.
bullets: Understanding: keyword matching, typos, cannot combine steps
Handover: cold transfer, customer repeats everything
Persisting: over-trust, interrogation, refusing to hand over
slides.example: CMR: 'no easy path to a human' is the single biggest irritant. Users type 'chicken nuggets' repeatedly to break out of loops.
slides.trap: Assuming handover problems are solved by better models. They persist because firms deploy bots to contain customers and cut cost.
slides.memorise: Group 1 understanding and complexity. Group 2 handover, humanisation, personalisation. Group 2 persists.
slides.notes: The professor splits chatbot failures into two groups. Group one is about understanding and complexity: the bot does not get what you mean, or cannot handle a two-part request. Generative AI largely fixed this. Group two is about the human side: cold handovers where you repeat everything, bots that sound robotic or fake-human, and answers that ignore who you are. These persist because expectations have risen, because firms over-trust the AI, and because bots are often designed to keep you away from expensive human agents. The CMR article says the number one irritant is simply having no easy path to a human.

slides.title: Three technical approaches
slides.definition: Off-the-shelf LLM, privately trained (fine-tuned) model, or off-the-shelf plus RAG. They differ in where the knowledge comes from.
bullets: Off-the-shelf: fastest, cheapest, generic, hallucinates company facts
Fine-tuned: deep brand knowledge, expensive, goes stale until retrained
RAG: fetches company documents at question time, current, citable
slides.example: Start-ups and fast-changing content use off-the-shelf + RAG (what Chatling does). Regulated enterprises fine-tune, often adding RAG too.
slides.trap: Believing fine-tuning keeps knowledge current. It freezes until retrained. RAG updates by changing a document, not the model.
slides.memorise: Off-the-shelf = fast but generic. Fine-tuned = deep but stale. RAG = current, cheap, citable. Most firms pick RAG.
slides.notes: Think of three ways to make a new employee useful. Off-the-shelf is hiring a smart generalist who knows nothing about your company: quick and cheap, but they will guess at your policies. Fine-tuning is sending them on months of training; they learn your tone and rules deeply, but their knowledge is frozen the day training ends, and retraining is costly. RAG is giving the generalist your manuals and letting them look things up before answering. It is current, cheap, and the answer can cite the page. RAG and fine-tuning are not rivals: fine-tuning teaches how to talk, RAG supplies what is true today.

slides.title: RAG: the open-book exam
slides.definition: Retrieval-augmented generation lets an LLM look up company documents before answering, grounding replies in real content with citations.
bullets: Ingestion: chunk documents, turn into embeddings, store in vector database
Retrieval: match the question, paste relevant chunks into the prompt
Can also query databases, call APIs, search the web
slides.example: McKinsey library analogy: ingestion stocks the shelves and builds the index; retrieval is the librarian finding the right pages.
slides.trap: Confusing RAG with fine-tuning. RAG does not update model parameters. It is only as good as the documents and the retrieval.
slides.memorise: RAG = ingestion then retrieval. Open-book exam. Garbage in, garbage out.
slides.notes: A normal LLM answers from memory, like a closed-book exam: it may be out of date or simply make things up. RAG turns it into an open-book exam. First comes ingestion: your FAQs, policies and product pages are cut into chunks and converted into embeddings, which are numbers that capture meaning, then stored so they can be searched by meaning. Then retrieval: the customer's question is matched to the most relevant chunks, which are pasted into the prompt. The model answers grounded in that text, often with a citation. The catch is garbage in, garbage out. If the manual is wrong, or the retrieval opens the wrong page, the answer is still wrong. So the real work becomes content governance.

slides.title: Psychology beats technology
slides.definition: Customers dislike chatbots for psychological reasons. Framing benefits, labelling, proof of accuracy and tone matter more than realism.
bullets: Knowing it is a bot: 8.5% less satisfaction, same conversation
Highlight benefits like instant and 24/7: plus 37% satisfaction
Humanisation is a dial: down for angry customers, up for good news
slides.example: HBR: 'constantly learning' label +17%; proof of accuracy +22%; angry customers 23% less satisfied with a human-like bot.
slides.trap: Thinking more realism fixes dislike. 73% mistook GPT-4.5 for a human, yet customers still dislike chatbots.
slides.memorise: Minus 8.5% for being a bot; plus 37% when benefits are framed. Be human, but do not pretend to be.
slides.notes: The HBR article's key study ran identical conversations and found satisfaction dropped 8.5% simply when people knew it was a chatbot. But when the bot's real strengths, instant and always available, were highlighted and delivered, satisfaction was 37% higher than with slower human agents. So the fix is framing, not realism. Call the bot constantly learning and people forgive errors like they would a keen new hire. Show accuracy statistics, because proof beats promises. Treat humanisation as a dial: angry or hurried customers want short, machine-like replies; good news should be delivered warmly; human-like phrasing in refund flows cuts lying by about 20%. And never pretend to be human.

Is this question descriptive, predictive or causal? What method follows?

slides.notes: Session 8 sits in the learn-and-control layer. Market research learns the market before acting; analytics monitors it constantly afterwards. AI has made analytics abundant, and this session is about why abundance is not quality. The goals ask you to define analytics, evaluate organisational models, judge when AI helps or hurts, separate three question types, and analyse unstructured data.

slides.title: Decision-grade analytics in six moves
bullets: Start with decision: Which decision will this change?
Label question: Descriptive, predictive or causal?
Expose assumptions: What would make this wrong?
Govern metrics: Define once, use everywhere
Validate high stakes: Review method, not just maths
Reward truth: Celebrate disconfirming evidence
slides.caption: Tadelis: answers are not evidence, and evidence is not a better decision. Add friction where being wrong is costly.

picture.title: Decision-grade analytics in six moves
picture.caption: Tadelis: answers are not evidence, and evidence is not a better decision. Add friction where being wrong is costly.

slides.notes: Tadelis's six principles form a sequence. Start with the decision, not the data. Label the question type so the method matches. Expose assumptions and ask what would make this wrong. Govern metrics so everyone means the same thing by churn or revenue. Validate high-stakes and causal claims in proportion to the stakes. Reward truth-seeking, not persuasion. Self-service analytics needs more governance, not less.

slides.title: Analytics ends in decisions
slides.definition: Marketing analytics is a technology-enabled, model-supported approach to harness customer and market data to enhance marketing decision making.
bullets: Definition ends with decision making, not data or insight
AI makes analysis faster, cheaper, open to citizen analysts
More answers do not mean better decisions
slides.example: Davenport & Bean five trends: agentic hype, measure GenAI, data culture, unstructured data, unsettled leadership. 92% cite culture as the barrier.
slides.trap: Thinking faster and cheaper analytics means better analytics. It means more efficient analytics; quality needs discipline.
slides.memorise: Analytics exists to improve decisions. Faster plus cheaper is efficiency, not quality.
slides.notes: Read the definition to the end: it finishes with decision making. That is the whole point of the session. AI has made analytics faster and cheaper and has opened it up to non-analysts, the so-called citizen analysts. But the professor's question is whether that implies better analytics, and the answer is no. Efficiency went up; decision quality only improves when the question is right, the method matches, and the metrics are governed. Davenport and Bean add that 92% of firms say culture and change management, not technology, are the main barrier.

slides.title: Centralised, embedded or hybrid
slides.definition: Analytics can sit in one central unit, inside business teams, or in a hybrid with a shared platform and embedded analysts sharing KPIs.
bullets: Centralised: standards, scale, governance; risks drifting from business
Embedded: context and speed; risks duplication and inconsistent metrics
Hybrid: central platform plus embedded teams sharing KPIs
slides.example: P&G: AI factory platform plus embedded data scientists, cuts deployment by about 6 months. DBS '2-in-a-box' shares KPIs with stakeholders.
slides.trap: Labelling DBS 2-in-a-box as centralised. It is a separate unit deeply embedded with stakeholders, sharing their KPIs.
slides.memorise: Hub owns platform and metric definitions; spokes sit in teams and share KPIs. CDO adoption 12% to 85%.
slides.notes: Technology and talent alone create no value; the insight has to reach the decision-maker. A centralised model under a Chief Data Officer gives consistent standards and scale but can become a cost centre that does not understand the business. An embedded model puts analysts inside brand or market teams, close to the problem, but duplicates work and defines churn three different ways. The hybrid takes the best of both: P&G's AI factory is a shared platform while most data scientists sit in business units. DBS keeps a separate analytics unit that is deeply embedded and shares the same KPIs as the business, fixing the old service-centre problem.

slides.title: Descriptive, predictive, causal
slides.definition: Descriptive asks what happened, predictive asks what will happen, causal asks what happens if we change something. Each needs a different method.
bullets: Descriptive: which campaign had the highest click-through rate?
Predictive: who will churn next month?
Causal: did the price cut cause the sales lift?
slides.example: Churn trap: 'Who is at risk?' is predictive; 'Whose behaviour changes if we intervene?' is causal. Different questions.
slides.trap: Labelling 'who will churn' as causal. Prediction is not intervention. AI answers both confidently even when the method is wrong.
slides.memorise: Causality needs three things: X before Y, X and Y associated, no competing explanations.
slides.notes: Before you trust any analysis, label the question. Descriptive looks back at what happened. Predictive forecasts what will happen if nothing changes. Causal asks what happens if we act. Most AI insights only establish association, which is condition two of three for causality. The three conditions are that X comes before Y, that X and Y move together, and that there is no competing explanation. That third condition is where selection bias hides. The exam loves this because an LLM will happily give a descriptive answer to a causal question, and a confident wrong answer scaled across thousands of campaigns is worse than no answer.

slides.title: Conversion is not incrementality
slides.definition: A high conversion rate may reflect who was targeted, not what the ad caused. Incrementality needs a control group.
bullets: Prospecting 3%, retargeting 10%: looks like shift budget
Retargeted users already intended to buy: selection bias
With controls: prospecting +2.0 pp, retargeting +0.5 pp
slides.example: eBay branded search ads looked effective; holdout experiments showed most value was not incremental because customers would have come anyway.
slides.trap: Recommending retargeting because 10% beats 3%. 95% of retargeting conversions would have happened without the ad.
slides.memorise: Prospecting 1% to 3% = +2.0 pp. Retargeting 9.5% to 10% = +0.5 pp. Compare cost per incremental conversion.
slides.notes: This is the slide most likely to appear in the exam. Prospecting converts at 3%, retargeting at 10%, so a typical LLM says move the budget to retargeting. That is a descriptive answer to a causal question. Retargeted people have already visited the site; many would buy anyway. Add control groups and the picture flips: prospecting lifts conversion from 1% to 3%, an incremental 2 points; retargeting lifts it from 9.5% to 10%, only half a point. Prospecting creates four times the lift per person. Then check cost per incremental conversion, because retargeting audiences are cheaper to reach, and keep some retargeting if it is still profitable. The quality of the answer came from the question and data design, not the AI.

slides.title: Unstructured data: text and images
slides.definition: Text and images have no ready-made variables. Someone must decide which features matter and validate AI scores against humans.
bullets: Text analytics: sentiment, topics, emotions
Images: low (colour, brightness), mid (objects, logos), high (emotion, aesthetics)
Pick the feature level that matches the decision
slides.example: Li & Xie Nike example: dark high-contrast background (low), product only (mid), 'high-performance' meaning (high). Boost reviews: lexicon misread sarcasm.
slides.trap: Calling logo detection low-level. Low is pixels (colour, contrast); mid is objects, faces, logos; high is interpretation.
slides.memorise: Low = colour, brightness, contrast. Mid = objects, people, logos. High = emotion, aesthetics, brand meaning.
slides.notes: Marketing is full of unstructured data: reviews, ads, packaging, social posts, chat logs. The key point from Li and Xie is that such data comes with no variables, so you must decide which features to extract. For images there are three levels. Low-level is what the pixels look like: colour, brightness, contrast. Mid-level is what is in the image: objects, faces, logos. High-level is how people interpret it: emotion, aesthetics, brand meaning. Do not extract everything; choose the level that matches the business outcome, and validate against human judgement. The Boost reviews exercise showed a lexicon tool scoring 'terrible experience' as positive because it saw the word 'better'. Check the method before trusting the number.

slides.title: Four kinds of Gen-AI risk (HBR 4 Ms)
bullets: Misuse: Scams, deepfakes, disinformation
Misrepresent: Knowingly spreading dubious AI content
Misapply: Trusting a hallucination (radio host lawsuit)
Misadventure: Unknowingly sharing a fake (Pentagon image)
slides.caption: Intent times usage: deliberate risks need policy and accountability; accidental risks need detection and review.

picture.title: Four kinds of Gen-AI risk (HBR 4 Ms)

slides.notes: The HBR four Ms grid crosses intent with usage. Creating content deliberately for harm is misuse: scams and deepfakes. Creating content and accidentally trusting a hallucination is misapply, like the lawsuit after ChatGPT falsely accused a radio host. Consuming and knowingly spreading dubious content is misrepresent. Consuming and unknowingly sharing a fake is misadventure, like the fake Pentagon explosion image. Mitigate creation with principles, watermarks and controlled environments; mitigate consumption with training, validation and a four-eye rule, and a damage plan.

slides.title: AI risk: inherited and added
slides.definition: AI risk is the probability times impact of deliberate or accidental harm to individuals, organisations or society from developing, deploying or using AI.
bullets: Inherited risk: created by the vendor (training data, objective, tuning)
Added risk: created by you (prompts, pasted data, what you publish)
You chose the vendor and chose to publish, so both land on you
slides.example: NEDA's Tessa chatbot gave dieting advice to eating-disorder sufferers; NEDA was blamed, not the vendor X2AI.
slides.trap: 'We only use the vendor's model, so the risk is theirs.' Not building the model does not remove your responsibility.
slides.memorise: Risk = probability x impact. Inherited from the vendor, added by you. Both are yours.
slides.notes: Start with the definition: risk is probability times impact, intent is deliberate or accidental, the victim is an individual, an organisation or society. Then the professor's key split. Inherited risk is baked in by the vendor: the training data, the labelling choices, the optimisation objective. You usually cannot see it. Added risk is what you introduce: what you prompt, what customer data you paste in, how much you edit versus rubber-stamp, what you publish. The slide's key line is that not building or training the model does not remove your responsibility. Customers, regulators and the media blame the brand. So do vendor due diligence, control your added risk, and keep records of human oversight.

slides.title: Three sources of bias
slides.definition: Algorithmic bias is systematic, repeatable error that disadvantages particular groups. It comes from biased data, non-representative data, or the wrong metric.
bullets: Biased training data: health algorithm used cost as proxy for need
Non-representative data: Gender Shades failed darker-skinned women
Wrong metric: STEM ad shown to more men because women cost more
slides.example: The STEM job ad was set gender-neutral; a cost-minimising algorithm bought cheaper male impressions. Perfect data, wrong objective.
slides.trap: Filing the STEM-ads case under biased data. The data were fine; the cost-minimising objective created the bias.
slides.memorise: Source 1 biased data (health cost proxy). Source 2 missing groups (Gender Shades). Source 3 wrong metric (STEM ads).
slides.notes: Bias is not the model being sometimes wrong; it is unfairness with a pattern. Three sources, each with a case you must be able to match. First, biased training data: a US health algorithm predicted cost as a proxy for need, but less is spent on Black patients at the same sickness level, so they were under-flagged. Removing race did not help because proxies carry the bias. Second, non-representative data: Gender Shades found face tools far worse for darker-skinned women because training sets were mostly lighter-skinned and male. Third, the wrong metric: a gender-neutral STEM ad reached more men because young women are a pricier audience and the algorithm minimised cost. In all three cases overall accuracy looked fine. You only see bias by disaggregating performance by subgroup.

slides.title: IP risk
slides.definition: Inherited IP risk asks whether the vendor could use its training data. Added IP risk asks whether the output you publish infringes.
bullets: Bartz v. Anthropic: legally acquired books fair use; pirated copies not
Getty v. Stability (UK): no copyright hit, but trademark via watermark
Purely AI output may not be copyrightable in the US
slides.example: Bartz drove a US$1.5bn settlement with authors. Getty's watermark reproduced in outputs was trademark infringement.
slides.trap: 'Getty won on copyright.' It did not: weights are not a copy and training was outside the UK; the win was trademark.
slides.memorise: Fair use is not a get-out-of-jail-free card. Keep records of prompts and human input; use indemnified tools.
slides.notes: Two layers again. Inherited: did the vendor have rights to the works it trained on? You cannot audit that, but you inherit the reputational and possibly legal exposure. Added: does what you publish infringe someone's copyright or trademark? That one is fully yours. The case law is moving fast. Bartz against Anthropic said training on legally bought books is fair use but pirated copies are not, leading to a 1.5 billion dollar settlement. Getty against Stability in the UK failed on copyright, since model weights are not a copy, but succeeded on trademark because outputs reproduced the Getty watermark. And purely AI-generated content may not be copyrightable, so competitors could reuse your ad. Manage it with licensed, indemnified tools, no 'in the style of' prompts, and logs of prompts and human edits.

slides.title: Privacy: leakage and inference
slides.definition: Privacy risk is inherited through memorised training data and added through data you paste in and sensitive attributes the system infers.
bullets: Input leakage: staff paste customer data into public AI tools
Inference: AI creates sensitive attributes nobody disclosed
Controls: data classification, minimisation, opt-outs, federated learning
slides.example: Samsung banned staff AI use after engineers leaked code into ChatGPT. Target predicted a teenager's pregnancy before her family knew.
slides.trap: Calling Target a data leak. No data leaked; the harm was inference, creating and acting on sensitive data.
slides.memorise: Samsung = input leakage. Target = inference. Inferred sensitive data is still sensitive.
slides.notes: Personalisation at scale means ever more personal data, so privacy risk grows in breadth and depth. Two added risks matter most. Input leakage: pasting customer records or code into a public tool, which may retain it or use it for training. Samsung's engineers did exactly that, and a ban followed. A ban is a short-term fix that pushes staff to shadow AI; better is approved enterprise tools plus a policy on which data categories may go into which tool. Inference: the system works out things people never told you, such as pregnancy or financial distress. Target's baby coupons revealed a pregnancy to the family. Legally grey, but it fails the reasonable-expectations test. Flag sensitive inferred categories, require opt-in, and do not build or sell such profiles.

slides.title: Governance and the risk map
slides.definition: AI governance monitors the whole workflow: classify risks as deliberate or accidental, map them by stakeholder and severity, and apply the matching controls.
bullets: Deliberate risk: policy, incentives, accountability controls
Accidental risk: detection, monitoring, review controls
Severity = likelihood x impact; map by stakeholder (Ethical Matrix)
slides.example: NIST AI RMF: Govern, Map, Measure, Manage. EU AI Act tiers: unacceptable, high, limited, minimal, based on use not technology.
slides.trap: Pairing deliberate risks with monitoring. A chosen trade-off needs policy and a named owner; monitoring catches the accidents.
slides.memorise: Deliberate -> policy and accountability. Accidental -> detection and review. Rows stakeholders, columns concerns, red/amber/green.
slides.notes: Governance means deciding in advance who checks what. First classify each risk. Deliberate means someone chose it or accepted a known trade-off, like a cost-minimising ad objective; fix it with policy, incentives and accountability. Accidental means nobody intended it; fix it with detection, monitoring and review such as red teaming and four-eye sign-off. Then map risks with the Ethical Matrix from MIT SMR: rows are stakeholders, split out vulnerable subgroups, columns are concerns, cells coloured red, amber or green by likelihood times impact. Harm to vulnerable groups or a legal hard constraint is automatically red. Two frameworks wrap it up: NIST's voluntary Govern, Map, Measure, Manage loop, and the binding EU AI Act, whose four tiers depend on how and where a system is used, not the technology itself. Chatbots and deepfakes sit in the limited tier with disclosure duties.

slides.notes: The reinvented campaign is a loop, not a line. Humans set the goal and guardrails at the top. A knowledge agent carries context, a planner pretests segments, content agents generate variants, a compliance agent checks rules written up front, an operator buys and shifts spend, and analytics feeds results straight back. The legal revision cycle and the post-campaign report are not sped up; they are absorbed.

slides.title: Agent vs assistant
slides.definition: An agentic workflow has AI agents that autonomously plan, execute and adapt tasks toward a goal using tools, data and other agents.
bullets: Four characteristics: goal-directed autonomy, planning, tool use, adaptivity
Assistant: human directs each step; output is content
Agent: operates from a goal; output is actions and outcomes
slides.example: Test: if nobody prompts it tomorrow, does work still get done? Assistant no; agent yes.
slides.trap: ChatGPT and Midjourney are assistants, not agents; the human still owns the workflow.
slides.memorise: Goal-directed autonomy, multi-step planning, tool use, adaptivity; agent owns part of the workflow.
slides.notes: Everything in Sessions 1 to 9 used AI as an assistant: you ask, it produces copy, an image or an analysis, and you decide the next step. An agent is different because you give it a goal, such as five thousand sign-ups under eight dollars each, and it plans the sub-tasks, calls tools like the ad platform and the CRM, acts, and adapts when results come in. MIT SMR calls it a tool that learns and a worker that is owned. Marketing suits agents because its work is repeatable but variable, data-rich, has fast feedback loops, and shows up directly in revenue and cost.

slides.title: The five-step design process
slides.definition: McKinsey's process: taxonomy of tasks → agent archetypes → agents needed → human role → prioritise in waves.
bullets: Taxonomy: break the workflow into microtasks and the systems behind them
Archetypes are reusable blueprints: content generator, knowledge, localization, analyzer, planner, operator
Integration, not model design, is the limiting factor; prioritise by readiness
slides.example: Consumer brand: hundreds of microtasks, six archetypes, ~100 modular agents, three waves, 4× faster.
slides.trap: Assuming the model is the bottleneck; McKinsey says system interoperability is.
slides.memorise: Taxonomy → archetypes → agents → human role → waves; six archetypes.
slides.notes: You cannot design the future workflow without understanding the present one, so step one is a detailed taxonomy of tasks and the systems they touch. Step two groups tasks into archetypes so you do not build a bespoke agent for everything. Step three picks the agents and checks they can plug into the CRM, content library and ad platforms, which is where most projects stall. Step four defines where humans add taste and oversight. Step five sequences waves by efficiency potential, growth goals and technical readiness.

slides.title: Agentizing vs reinventing
slides.definition: Agentizing adds agents to existing steps so the same process runs faster; reinventing redesigns the workflow as if agents had always existed.
bullets: Agentization trap: efficiency without structural gain; 'paving the cow paths'
Old steps reflect human limits that agents remove ('there is no spoon')
Reinvention eliminates steps and collapses organisational boundaries
slides.example: Legacy insurer: form → underwriter → pricing → quote, hours to days. Lemonade's Maya: underwriting inside the agent, ~90 seconds.
slides.trap: A faster line is a retrofit, not reinvention; ask whether steps vanished and the shape changed.
slides.memorise: Agentize = same shape faster; reinvent = steps eliminated, boundaries collapsed, line to loop.
slides.notes: This is the heart of the session and the professor's own sample exam question. Most firms drop agents into each step of today's workflow and get the same process a bit faster. The slides use the Matrix line, there is no spoon, to say that the steps we treat as fixed were designed around human constraints. Reinvention asks how we would design this today. Lemonade did not speed up its underwriters; it removed the underwriting stage by putting the decision inside the agent. In class we did the same to the campaign workflow: the legal revision cycle and the post-campaign analytics disappeared and the line became a loop.

slides.title: Who benefits: five forces
slides.definition: HBR's five forces shift advantage from scale of resources to speed of learning, favouring AI-native startups but leaving incumbents real assets.
bullets: Zero-latency iteration; automated go-to-market; autonomous functions
Radical capital efficiency; AI-driven flywheel of compounding knowledge
Incumbents keep distribution, trust, data, domain experts; must re-architect before automating
slides.example: Six-to-eight person product teams become two people; Series A on $2m, 80% less; Lemonade's risk knowledge cannot be copied.
slides.trap: Saying startups win outright; incumbents keep trust, distribution and experts.
slides.memorise: Five forces: iteration, go-to-market, autonomous functions, capital efficiency, flywheel.
slides.notes: Incumbents used to win on scale: capital, people, data, distribution and time to build systems. The first two forces collapse time and cost to market, the next two collapse headcount and funding, and the flywheel rewards deep workflow knowledge over size. So startups benefit first and most. But incumbents are not finished: they keep brand trust, distribution, proprietary data, a compliance record and the domain experts agentic systems need. Their most common mistake is automating before re-architecting.

slides.title: Chained risks and humans in the loop
slides.definition: Linked agents create chained, cascading risks; humans belong at approval gates, exception handling and audit or override, not everywhere.
bullets: Five drivers: chained vulnerabilities, cross-agent escalation, synthetic identity, untraceable leakage, data corruption
Agents are 'digital insiders'; cause is interconnection without checks
Controls: agent identity and access management, logging, sandboxes, kill switch
slides.example: Credit-data agent misclassifies debt as income; scoring and approval agents grant a risky loan. 80% of organisations report risky agent behaviour.
slides.trap: Approving every agent action recreates the old chain; removing humans ignores cascading risk.
slides.memorise: Approval gates, exception handling, audit and override; judgment where it adds value or manages risk.
slides.notes: Session 9 looked at one system's bias, IP and privacy risks. Agents add a new dimension because they are linked: a flaw in one cascades and is amplified downstream, a compromised agent can abuse the trust others give it, identities can be forged, data moves between agents without logs, and bad data spreads silently. The answer is not humans everywhere, which would be the agentization trap in governance form, but humans placed deliberately: sign-off before high-stakes actions, escalation of unusual cases, and the ability to audit, reverse and retrain. MIT SMR calls this the supervision-versus-autonomy tension.

slides.title: Heterogeneity is the problem
slides.definition: People buy the same product for different reasons, so one average message speaks to nobody; personalisation answers that.
bullets: Different emotional triggers need different visual and textual cues
This is STP from Session 1 pushed to the creative level
The product does not change; only the message does
slides.example: Nespresso: iced café treat for Gen Z, 10 quiet minutes for parents, fair-price upgrade for switchers.
slides.trap: Thinking personalisation means a new product per segment; it is the same machine with a different job to do.
slides.memorise: Same machine, three jobs: belonging/esteem, self-care, value.
slides.notes: The brief starts from a simple observation: a single average message converts poorly because customers are heterogeneous. One person buys a coffee machine to feel like a café regular, another to carve out ten quiet minutes, another because it is good value. The product is identical; the need is not. That is exactly Session 1's logic of value and STP, now applied to one ad per segment. The professor is testing whether you can trace a creative decision back to a human motivation.

slides.title: Research you can defend
slides.definition: Synthetic market research must be documented and reproducible: questions asked, number of participants, method of analysis, and limits.
bullets: 150 respondents, 14 questions, 6 independent chats of 25
Two independent analyst runs with an 88% agreement check
Closed counts cross-checked against raw data; one miscount corrected
slides.example: Limitations stated: template repetition, 85% female skew, halal only among Malay personas, polite answers.
slides.trap: Presenting synthetic percentages as findings; the brief and Session 2 require treating them as hypotheses.
slides.memorise: Say what you asked, how many, how analysed, and that the data are simulated.
slides.notes: Marks for Section 2 come from rigour and honesty. You must state the questions, the sample size, how the data were generated and how they were analysed. The strong move is independence: separate chats so personas do not copy each other, and two analyst passes compared against each other. Then be specific about limitations, because that is what the professor asked in Session 2 with 'do you believe the results?'. A limitation that leads to a decision, such as no gender or ethnic targeting because of skew, is worth more than a generic caveat.

slides.title: Usable segments
slides.definition: A segment is usable when it is sizeable, valuable, truly different in response, and identifiable on a real ad platform.
bullets: Identifiability on Meta: custom audiences, interests, life events, lookalikes
Explain rejected segments: too small, too similar, not targetable
Give each segment a funnel role: acquire, retain, convert
slides.example: Owners vs non-owners via CRM lists, Dolce Gusto owners via interests, new parents via life events, 11.11 timing.
slides.trap: Keeping a psychologically interesting segment that no platform can reach; the brief calls these unusable.
slides.memorise: Size, value, distinctiveness, identifiability – all four, or drop the segment.
slides.notes: The targeting step of STP has a practical test here: can Meta actually deliver a different ad to these people? You must name the signals, such as custom audiences from CRM data, interest targeting, life events or lookalike seeds. If a segment is fascinating but not reachable, it fails. You also show judgement by explaining which candidate segments you dropped and why. Giving each kept segment a job in the funnel, acquisition, retention or conversion, shows the choice is strategic.

slides.title: Motivation → creative link
slides.definition: Randomly changing a colour or a face is not personalisation; each creative lever must trace to the segment's motivation with evidence.
bullets: Hold brand elements constant: logo, product with capsules, format, one CTA
Vary need, occasion, people shown, palette, composition, copy, CTA
Contrast check: why the other two segments would scroll past
slides.example: 'Your 10 minutes, sorted' is a verbatim from respondent 1; price badge answers 'no price = annoying'.
slides.trap: Two ads that look nearly the same; the marker cannot see the segment logic, so it reads as three random designs.
slides.memorise: Constant brand + varied need-linked levers = personalisation you can prove.
slides.notes: This is the highest-weight section and the heart of the brief. Personalisation must be a genuine link between what the segment wants and what the ad shows and says. Holding the brand elements constant is the clever part: if logo, product and format never change, every remaining difference must be segment logic. Then each lever, from the Maslow need to the CTA, is justified with a quote or a number from your research. Finish with a contrast check that explains why segment A would ignore segment B's ad. Cosmetic variation earns nothing.

slides.title: Validate and govern
slides.definition: Close the loop: test that each segment prefers its ad, plan a real experiment, and add the risk and AI-disclosure items.
bullets: Synthetic ad test: personas pick which ad stops the scroll; aim for 60%+ choosing 'their' ad
Real validation: Meta A/B test with a control ad on CTR and incremental sales
Appendix: AI-tool disclosure, prompts, invented offers and logo use noted
slides.example: Prompt E in the prompt pack: 20 personas per segment judge three ads described in words.
slides.trap: Measuring success with likes; Session 8 says use incrementality, and simulated data need human checks.
slides.memorise: Synthetic test → real A/B with control → disclose AI use and limits.
slides.notes: A good report becomes a top report when it tests itself. Reuse the personas to run a quick ad test and report the result honestly, including when a segment prefers another ad and what you changed. Then say how a real team would validate: an A/B test on Meta with the three ads in three audiences plus a control average ad, measured on click-through and incremental sales rather than likes, followed by real interviews. Finally the governance pieces from Session 9: disclose which AI tools did what, keep prompts and human checks, and flag stereotyped imagery, IP and inference risks.
